books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Challenging Child Labor
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: Lewis Hine, photographs of child workers, c. 1908-1911

stimulus.source_note: Photograph by Lewis Hine, c. 1911, public domain (pre-1930). Caption per the source record.
stimulus.text: Photograph by Lewis Hine, 1911. A young girl in a plain dress stands outdoors and looks directly at the camera. Hine's caption records her as a girl working in a cannery.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: Hine took photographs like this one mainly to

options.text: advertise the products of American factories to buyers
options.misconception: Hine worked for reform groups, not for factory owners selling goods.

options.text: celebrate the progress and success of American industry
options.misconception: The photograph shows a child worker, not industrial triumph; Hine meant it as an indictment.

options.text: show the public child labor conditions and build support for reform
recruit more children to work in the mills and factories
options.misconception: Hine's photographs argued against child labor; they did not recruit children into it.

rationales.A: Hine worked for reform organizations. His photographs indicted factories; they did not sell their products.
rationales.B: The picture shows a young girl at work, not a triumph of industry. Hine's point was the cost of that industry.
rationales.C: Hine photographed child workers so the public could see them. His pictures were published to build support for laws limiting child labor, and reformers used them for exactly that purpose.
rationales.D: Hine's work argued against child labor. Recruiting children into the mills would reverse his purpose.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who hired the photographer. Hine worked for reformers, not for factory owners.
2. Ask what the picture is for. A young girl facing the camera shows the public a child laborer, not a product.
3. Rule out the reversals. Advertising, celebration, and recruiting all serve the factories, not the reform.
Remember: a photograph's purpose follows its sponsor, so ask who wanted the picture taken and why.
